All topics · Indian History · Lesson 5

Cities, the Buddha and the first empire

Two sittings (read ~25 min one day, lesson ~25 min the next). One win: judge the claim "Chanakya was India's Machiavelli" from the book itself.

Why this lesson

By about 1000 BC the Vedic people were farming the Ganga–Yamuna Doab and had no cities. Seven hundred years later a single state ruled from Afghanistan to Bengal, with a capital that may have been the largest city in the world. Between those two points sit three things this lesson connects: new cities on the Ganges, a new religion (the Buddha's), and India's first empire (the Mauryas). The question to carry through: why did all three happen in the same place, the eastern Ganges plain, at about the same time?

Warm-up (4 minutes)

Answer these from memory; the recap after them has the answers.

Place the end of the great Indus cities (within 150 years). Bare years on this timeline are read as BCE.

K&R date the mature cities 2600–1700 BC. That leaves roughly a thousand years with no cities before the Ganges towns of this lesson.

The Rigveda's words were passed down orally with great accuracy. Which statement best describes it as a source on Vedic society?

Both halves matter. Faithful oral transmission makes the text "a fairly reliable source", but these texts "express the priestly world-view of the Brahmins". So the Purusha hymn, which puts Brahmins at the top, may describe the order the priests wanted, not how everyone lived.

The four broad ranked estates of the Late Vedic texts are the [[varnas|varna]]; the caste a person is born into, one of hundreds, is their [[jati|jatis]].

Varna first meant "colour" and became four estates (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra); jati comes from jata, "born".

Recap: the two earlier ages this lesson builds on
  • The Indus cities (c. 2600–1700 BC): planned brick cities with standard weights, gone well before the Vedic hymns. After them, India had no cities for about a thousand years.
  • The Vedic age (Rigveda c. 1300–1000 BC): our evidence is the priests' own hymns. By the Late Vedic age, the priests (Brahmins) and warrior-rulers (Kshatriyas) sat at the top of a ranked order of four varnas (estates); the many birth-castes, jatis, came much later.

Block 1: read first

Reading

Kulke & Rothermund, A History of India, Chapter Two, "Ancient Kingdoms and Empires". Two slices, about 8 pages:

  1. "Urbanisation in the Ganges valley" and "The rise of Buddhism" (about 3 pages). Stop at "The west under Persian domination".
  2. Jump to "Alexander's Indian campaign" and read straight through "The foundation of the Maurya empire" and "The political system of the Arthashastra", including the boxed quotation "Rajamandala, an image of early Indian geo-politics". Stop at "Ashoka, the Beloved of the Gods" (about 5 pages).

Optional, if you have time: the two sections you skipped, "The west under Persian domination" and "The origins of the early state" (about 3½ pages). They explain how Magadha beat its rivals; the lesson summarises what you need.

Name traps: the book spells the author of the Arthashastra Kautalya. Most people say Kautilya or Chanakya: the same figure, as far as tradition goes. Greek names come in Greek spelling: Poros (Porus), Seleukos (Seleucus), the river Hydaspes (today's Jhelum).

Answer the boxes below as you read, a sentence or two each. They're your notes; every answer gets a reply.

What evidence do K&R give that real cities grew up on the Ganges plain after 600 BC? Name two kinds, and one thing a city culture usually has that hasn't been found there yet.

Any two of: fortifications (moats, earth ramparts, later brick walls; Kausambi's 4-mile walls), punch-marked coins, standardised weights, Northern Black Polished Ware spreading along trade routes, assembly halls, kiln-fired bricks again; five of six big cities were capitals of mahajanapadas. Missing: a script (Ashoka's inscriptions, 3rd century BC, are the earliest). Reading note, not graded for mastery.

Why do K&R think the Buddha may have lived a century later than the traditional date?

The traditional dates (544 BC; 483 BC long accepted by historians) rest on later Buddhist chronicles; Bechert argued (1980s) they can't be trusted and the Buddha may have lived about a century later; early Buddhist texts (Jatakas) describe a flourishing urban society, and archaeology suggests that only existed in the 5th century, not the 6th. Credit for either the chronicle point or the cities point.

What do K&R say the Arthashastra is a good source for, and why might it not describe the Maurya empire as it really was?

It describes several small rival kingdoms competing, which fits the mahajanapada period before Magadha won, so it is better read as a normative account of state formation in that earlier period (and of medieval India, where rival kingdoms were typical), than as a picture of Chandragupta's empire. Also: parts are later additions, perhaps as late as AD 300. Either point.

What surprised or confused you in the reading?

No right answer. Reply to it.

Block 2: the lesson

1. Cities and the Buddha, together (from the reading)

Start from what's solid. After 600 BC the Ganges plain had cities again: five of the six big ones were capitals of mahajanapadas ("great tribal realms", sixteen rival kingdoms and republics). Historians call this the second urbanisation (the Indus cities were the first); K&R don't use the phrase, but it's the standard name you'll meet elsewhere.

Now the question: why would a new religion appear in exactly these places? Try to answer it before opening the steps. The first and third steps are from the reading; the second is beyond it.

Who was the Buddha talking back to? K&R call Buddhism "a reaction to the Brahmin–Kshatriya alliance of the Late Vedic age". The Vedic order put priests and their sacrifices at the top. A teaching that offered release from suffering through conduct, not ritual, undercut the priests' monopoly.

Who listened? (beyond the reading) Coins and standard weights tell us there was money and long-distance trade, so the cities held traders and craftsmen, people with wealth but no high place in the Vedic ranking. K&R don't spell this out, but they give the clues: the Buddha preached in these towns and met kings like Bimbisara of Magadha, the towns soon held monasteries and stupas, and Jainism, its sister movement, kept its base "in the rich merchant communities of western India".

The dating clue runs the other way, too. The earliest Buddhist stories already describe busy cities. Archaeology shows the Gangetic cities only beginning in the 6th century BC and flourishing in the 5th, so that's one reason to move the Buddha later (the German scholar Heinz Bechert's argument). The religion and the cities are so tied together that each helps date the other.

So: K&R's own sentence is that the new Gangetic civilisation "found its spiritual expression" in a reform movement against the Brahmin–Kshatriya alliance. The new urban society was the setting, and (beyond the reading) very likely the audience, for a teaching about conduct rather than sacrifice.

Which statement best matches K&R's explanation of how Buddhism relates to the new Ganges cities?

K&R: the new Gangetic civilisation "found its spiritual expression in a reform movement which was a reaction to the Brahmin–Kshatriya alliance of the Late Vedic age". The Persians ruled the far northwest, not the Ganges; and the reform turned away from sacrifice.

Did the Ganges cities have this in the 6th–5th centuries BC, according to K&R?

Coins, weights and fortifications are all there. No script yet: Ashoka's inscriptions, 3rd century BC, are the earliest Indian writing (though the scripts were so developed they probably began earlier). And planned street networks start again only in the 4th century BC.

2. From kingdoms to an empire (from the reading, and the optional sections)

Magadha, one of the sixteen mahajanapadas, rose to dominate the Ganges plain within two generations, and its later rulers kept expanding. K&R list the steps: Bimbisara conquered neighbouring Anga (and its access to iron ore and trade routes); his son Ajatashatru's generals fortified Pataligrama, a village on the Ganga that became Pataliputra (today's Patna), about 380 km downriver (east) of Kausambi; the Nandas built the first huge army (Greek reports say 3,000 elephants); then Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the last Nanda.

Alexander matters to this story mostly by what he didn't do. He crossed the Indus in 326 BC, beat Poros at the Hydaspes, and then his army refused to go further east, where "more kings and war elephants were waiting". Indian sources don't even mention him. But Chandragupta, says tradition, began by fighting the outposts Alexander left behind.

When did the Mauryas begin? Work it out from three dates in the reading before looking.

Alexander's army was in the Panjab in 326 BC and the Nandas still ruled Magadha. By 317 BC the last Greek outposts in India were gone.

K&R: Chandragupta "seems to have usurped the throne of Magadha in 320 BC" (many books say 321 or 322; the sources disagree by a year or two).

In 305 BC Seleukos, heir to Alexander's eastern conquests, invaded; Chandragupta stopped him, and Seleukos ceded everything east of Kabul for 500 elephants. The Maurya frontier was then roughly the Mughal frontier two thousand years later.

Click where Pataliputra, the Nanda and Maurya capital, stood: on the Ganga, about 380 km east of Kausambi (within 200 km).

Pataliputra is modern Patna, on the Ganga in Bihar, in the old heartland of Magadha.

Put these in order, earliest first.

Bimbisara (the Buddha's contemporary, 5th century BC) → Alexander (326 BC) → Chandragupta (c. 320 BC) → the treaty with Seleukos (305 BC).

Place the start of the Maurya empire, when Chandragupta took the throne of Magadha (within 20 years).

c. 320 BC (K&R; other books give 321 or 322). Six years after Alexander crossed the Indus, fifteen before the treaty with Seleukos.

3. Megasthenes: checking a foreign witness (from the reading)

Seleukos sent an ambassador, Megasthenes, to Pataliputra. His book is lost, but later Greek writers quoted it. He said the city's palisade ran about 21 miles around, with 570 towers and 64 gates: twice the size of Marcus Aurelius's Rome. An ambassador has a motive to exaggerate the court he was sent to. So how could a historian test him?

Why do K&R take Megasthenes' size for Pataliputra more seriously than you might expect?

D. Schlingloff showed that the gaps between towers and gates in Megasthenes' account match the 54 yards that the Arthashastra prescribes. Two sources with different authors and purposes agree: that's corroboration, and it's why a historian's trust goes up.

4. The Arthashastra's circle of kings (from the reading)

The Arthashastra, "the science of prosperity" (artha), is a manual for a king, traditionally by Chandragupta's minister Kautilya. Its picture of the world is the rajamandala, the circle of kings. Reason it out first: if you're a king among many small kingdoms, who is your natural enemy, and who is your natural friend?

Your neighbour is your enemy (ari). You share a border, so you compete for the same land; either of you gains by swallowing the other.

Your neighbour's neighbour is your friend (mitra). The kingdom on the far side of your enemy has the same enemy you do. "The enemy of my enemy". Kautilya: "one with territory separated by one [other territory] is … the ally."

The pattern repeats outward: beyond the ally lies the enemy's ally, then the ally's ally, then the enemy's ally's ally. In front and behind you, enemies and friends alternate.

Two kings break the pattern. The middle king (madhyama) borders both you and your enemy and is strong enough to stay neutral or decide your war by joining one side. The neutral king (udasina, "the great outsider") sits outside the whole circle, stronger than any of you, and can interfere anywhere: K&R say he "was to be carefully watched".

This is the same "enemy of my enemy" logic you'll meet in the strategy course as balance-of-power thinking.

The king wins by building up his seven factors of power (himself, ministers, provinces, city, treasury, army, allies) and wearing down the enemy's before any battle: irrigation, trade, mines, forts, elephants, and spies.

Kingdoms lie in a row. You are at one end. Counting outward, the 1st kingdom is your neighbour. By Kautilya's pattern, which is the nearest kingdom beyond your ally that is also friendly to you? Type its position in the row (1 = your neighbour).

1 enemy, 2 ally (mitra), 3 the enemy's ally, 4 the ally's ally. Friends sit at even positions, enemies at odd ones.

Kingdoms A and B, neighbours, are at war. Kingdom C borders both and is strong enough to stay out of it or to decide it by joining either side. What does Kautilya call C? (Either the Sanskrit term or its English translation.)

The middle king (madhyama). The neutral king (udasina) is different: he sits outside the circle altogether.

5. The claim: "Chanakya was India's Machiavelli"

You'll hear this often. The sociologist Max Weber made the strongest version in 1919: next to the Arthashastra, he said, Machiavelli's The Prince is harmless. Judge it from the reading. Keep in mind three facts K&R give: spies take up many pages; the text's real focus is a prosperous economy run by the state; and the king must keep his subjects content, because high taxes and forced labour "would drive the population into the arms of the enemy".

Beyond the reading, one more caution about the name: the Arthashastra calls its author Kautilya, and tradition makes him the same man as Chanakya, Chandragupta's minister. Many scholars now doubt that. K&R keep the older view: Kautilya lived around 300 BC and later hands added to his text, some as late as AD 300. The newer view (Patrick Olivelle's 2013 edition) puts the composition of most of the text itself in the first centuries AD.

Using the reading, give (1) one way the comparison with Machiavelli fits, (2) one way K&R say it misleads, and (3) one reason the Arthashastra may not describe Chandragupta's real empire. Then give your verdict on the claim, in a sentence.

Grades exactly the three named parts, from K&R Ch. 2 only. (1) Fits: detailed, amoral advice on spies and secret agents with "great psychological insight into the weakness of human nature"; "no moral limits" to exploiting the surplus; the enemy/ally logic is pure power calculation. Any one. (2) Misleads: K&R say Kautilya "paid less attention to clandestine activities in the enemy's territory than to the elimination of 'thorns' in the king's own country"; most of the book is economics and administration (mining, trade, crafts, agriculture, salaries); and it limits power by feasibility (subjects' welfare and contentment). Any one. (3) Not a picture of the empire: it describes many rival small kingdoms, like the mahajanapada period before Magadha's victory, so it's normative and about state formation; parts were added later (to AD 300). Either. Verdict: any reasoned verdict. Got it = all three parts, no false statement. (Authorship doubts are beyond the reading: credit, never required.)

Extra practice (optional)

  • Reading: the boxed source "Rajamandala, an image of early Indian geo-politics" once more, slowly: which kings does Kautilya say to "exterminate", which to "harass", and what decides it? (K&R Ch. 2.)
  • Extra reading: Damien Keown, Buddhism: A Very Short Introduction (in your library), Chapter 2, "The Buddha" (about 8 pages). A specialist's view of the life, with the later death date (around 410 BC) that matches K&R's argument.
  • Extra article: "Key thinker: Kautilya", from Oxford's Rethinking Political Thinkers resources (about 1,000 words). It starts from Weber's comparison and argues Kautilya was as concerned with good and bad politics as with power. A short, opposite view to test your verdict against. Read it on Oxford Learning Link.
